title: Sequences, Triangular Patterns & Rules: Explicit Formulas vs Recursive Relations
description: Formulate mathematical sequences as ordered lists of numbers obeying a deterministic rule. Contrast explicit formulas t_n = f(n) with recursive definitions t_{n+1} = g(t_n). Explore figurate triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2 and their geometric dot patterns.
subtopics: Definition of a sequence: Ordered terms t_1, t_2, ..., t_n indexed by natural numbers
Figurate numbers: Visualizing triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2 with geometric dot arrays
Pairing consecutive triangular numbers to produce square numbers: T_n + T_{n-1} = n^2
Explicit rules: Direct evaluation of arbitrary terms (e.g. t_n = 3n - 7, finding 1170th term)
Recursive rules: Defining subsequent terms from predecessors (e.g. t_1 = 1, t_{n+1} = t_n + n + 1)
Testing sequence membership: Determining if a given integer belongs to a sequence
key_concepts: Sequence Definition: A mapping from the set of natural numbers {1, 2, 3, ...} to real numbers, denoted as {t_n}.
Explicit Formula Invariant: Expresses t_n purely in terms of its position index n. Allows instant calculation of ANY term (such as t_1000) in O(1) time without computing prior terms.
Recursive Formula Invariant: Expresses t_{n+1} using one or more preceding terms (t_n, t_{n-1}) along with an initial base condition t_1.
Triangular Number Formula: T_n = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2. Geometrically represented by packing an n x (n+1) rectangle with two congruent triangular dot arrays.
Consecutive Triangular Square Theorem: T_n + T_{n-1} = n(n+1)/2 + (n-1)n/2 = n/2 * (n + 1 + n - 1) = n/2 * (2n) = n^2.
success_criteria: Generate terms from explicit and recursive rules, calculate triangular numbers, and test whether numbers belong to a given sequence.
chapter_notes: Triangular numbers provide the vital geometric hook for sequences in Ganita Manjari. Point out how two copies of T_n fit together into an n by (n+1) rectangle.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook In-Text Exercise: Consider the explicit rule t_n = 3n - 7. (i) Find its 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 12th, 18th, and 50th terms. (ii) Which term of the sequence is 332? (iii) Is 557 a term of this sequence? Explain why or why not.
worked_examples.formula: Substitute n into t_n = 3n - 7. To test membership, solve 3n - 7 = Target for natural number n.
worked_examples.calculation:
Part (i):
  t_1 = 3(1) - 7 = 3 - 7 = -4
  t_2 = 3(2) - 7 = 6 - 7 = -1
  t_3 = 3(3) - 7 = 9 - 7 = 2
  t_12 = 3(12) - 7 = 36 - 7 = 29
  t_18 = 3(18) - 7 = 54 - 7 = 47
  t_50 = 3(50) - 7 = 150 - 7 = 143.

Part (ii):
  Set t_n = 332:
  3n - 7 = 332
  3n = 332 + 7 = 339
  n = 339 / 3 = 113.
  Since 113 is a positive integer, 332 IS the 113th term of the sequence.

Part (iii):
  Set t_n = 557:
  3n - 7 = 557
  3n = 557 + 7 = 564
  n = 564 / 3 = 188.
  Since 188 is a positive integer, 557 IS the 188th term of the sequence.

title: Arithmetic Progressions (AP): Common Difference, General Term t_n = a + (n-1)d & Linear Plots
description: Establish Arithmetic Progressions where each term differs from the previous by a constant difference d. Derive the general nth term formula t_n = a + (n-1)d. Prove that plotting (n, t_n) on Cartesian axes produces collinear points on a line of slope d.
subtopics: Formal definition of an AP: t_{n+1} - t_n = d (constant for all n >= 1)
Common difference d: Positive (increasing AP), Negative (decreasing AP), Zero (constant AP)
Derivation of the general term: t_n = a + (n - 1)d
Linear correspondence: t_n = dn + (a - d) is a linear function with slope d
Textbook Taxi Fare Model (Example 5): Fixed fee Rs 200 + Rs 40/km
Determining whether a given sequence is an AP by checking consecutive differences
key_concepts: Common Difference Invariant: An AP is uniquely determined by two parameters: first term a and common difference d = t_{k+1} - t_k.
General Term Formula: t_n = a + (n - 1)d. The factor is (n - 1), because the first term already accounts for 1 step, requiring (n - 1) further jumps of d.

Linear Graph Equivalence: When plotted on a Cartesian plane with horizontal axis n and vertical axis t_n, the points (n, t_n) lie strictly on a straight line whose slope is identically equal to the common difference d.
Recursive AP Rule: t_1 = a, t_{n+1} = t_n + d.
success_criteria: Verify if sequences are APs, compute general terms, find specific distant terms, and explain the slope-difference equivalence.
chapter_notes: Connect Chapter 8 directly back to Chapter 1 & 2! The slope of the line in Chapter 2 is exactly the common difference d of the AP in Chapter 8.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Exercise 8.2 Q1 & Q2: (Q1) Find the 10th and 26th terms of the AP: 3, 8, 13, 18, ... (Q2) Which term of the AP: 21, 18, 15, ... is -81? Also, is 0 a term of this AP?
worked_examples.calculation:
Part (Q1):
Step 1: First term a = 3, common difference d = 8 - 3 = 5.
Step 2: 10th term: t_10 = a + 9d = 3 + 9(5) = 3 + 45 = 48.
Step 3: 26th term: t_26 = a + 25d = 3 + 25(5) = 3 + 125 = 128.

Part (Q2):
Step 1: a = 21, d = 18 - 21 = -3.
Step 2: Find n such that t_n = -81:
  21 + (n - 1)(-3) = -81
  (n - 1)(-3) = -81 - 21 = -102
  n - 1 = -102 / -3 = 34
  n = 34 + 1 = 35.
  Therefore, -81 is the 35th term.
Step 3: Test if 0 is a term:
  21 + (n - 1)(-3) = 0
  (n - 1)(-3) = -21
  n - 1 = 7 => n = 8.
  Since n is a positive integer, 0 IS the 8th term of the AP.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Q1: t_10 = 48, t_26 = 128; Q2: -81 is the 35th term, and 0 is the 8th term

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5 (Taxi Fare Model): A taxi company charges a fixed booking fee of Rs 200 plus Rs 40 per kilometre travelled. Write the sequence representing the total fare after 1 km, 2 km, 3 km, and find the fare for travelling 25 km.
worked_examples.given: Fixed fee = Rs 200, Rate per km = Rs 40/km.
worked_examples.formula: Fare sequence: F_n = 200 + 40n. This is an AP with first term a = 240 and d = 40.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Write terms for initial kilometres:
  After 1 km: 200 + 40 = Rs 240.
  After 2 km: 200 + 40(2) = Rs 280.
  After 3 km: 200 + 40(3) = Rs 320.
  Sequence: 240, 280, 320, 360, ...
Step 2: Check common difference:
  280 - 240 = 40; 320 - 280 = 40. Constant d = 40, so it is an AP.
Step 3: Calculate fare for 25 km:
  F_25 = 200 + 40 * 25 = 200 + 1000 = Rs 1,200.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Sequence: 240, 280, 320, ... (AP with a=240, d=40); Fare for 25 km = Rs 1,200

common_misconceptions: Writing t_n = a + nd instead of a + (n - 1)d, which mistakenly adds one extra step of d.
Getting the sign of d wrong in decreasing sequences (e.g. 21, 18, 15... has d = -3, not +3).

questions.question: What is the common difference d of the AP: -5, -1, 3, 7, ...?
questions.socratic_hint: Subtract the first term from the second term.

questions.question: Why is the coefficient of (n - 1) in t_n = a + (n - 1)d equal to (n - 1) instead of n?
questions.ideal_answer: Because the first term t_1 = a requires 0 steps of d. Each subsequent term advances by one step of d, so the nth term requires exactly (n - 1) steps.
questions.socratic_hint: How many steps of d do you add to get from the 1st term to the nth term?

questions.question: Find the 20th term of the AP whose first term is 7 and common difference is -4.
questions.socratic_hint: Use t_20 = a + 19d.

questions.question: If the 7th term of an AP is 34 and the 13th term is 64, find the common difference d.
questions.socratic_hint: Subtract t_7 from t_13 to eliminate a.

questions.question: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3?
questions.ideal_answer: First two-digit number divisible by 3 is 12; last is 99. The sequence is 12, 15, 18, ..., 99 (an AP with a = 12, d = 3). Formula: t_n = a + (n - 1)d => 99 = 12 + (n - 1)(3) => 87 = 3(n - 1) => n - 1 = 29 => n = 30 two-digit numbers.
questions.socratic_hint: Find the smallest two-digit multiple of 3 and largest, then solve for n.

title: Arithmetic Series: Gauss Summation Formula S_n = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d] & Practical Sums
description: Formulate the sum of an arithmetic series by reversing and pairing terms (Gauss's discovery). Derive both forms S_n = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d] and S_n = n/2 [a + l]. Deduce the sum of the first n natural numbers and first n odd integers.
subtopics: Young Carl Friedrich Gauss's famous classroom insight: Sum of 1 to 100 = 5050
Derivation of the general AP sum formula by writing S_n forward and backward
Pairwise summation: 2*S_n = n * (a + l) where l is the last term
First form: S_n = (n/2) * [2a + (n - 1)d]
Second form: S_n = (n/2) * [first term + last term]
Sum of first n natural numbers: Σ n = n(n+1)/2; Sum of first n odd numbers: Σ (2k-1) = n^2
key_concepts: Gauss Pairing Invariant: In any AP, the sum of terms equidistant from the beginning and end is constant: t_1 + t_n = t_2 + t_{n-1} = ... = a + l = 2a + (n - 1)d.
Series Sum Invariants: S_n = n/2 * (a + l) = n/2 * [2a + (n - 1)d].
Sum of Natural Numbers: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2. Direct algebraic equivalent of triangular numbers T_n.
Odd Numbers Square Theorem: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n/2 * [1 + (2n - 1)] = n/2 * (2n) = n^2. Geometrically corresponds to nested L-shaped gnomons forming concentric squares.
success_criteria: Derive the Gauss summation formula, compute sums of APs using both formulas, and solve practical series problems.
chapter_notes: Gauss's proof is one of the most beautiful in school mathematics. Have students write S_n forwards and backwards on their chalkboards to see the identical pairs emerge.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Derivation & Gauss Problem: (i) Find the sum of the first 100 positive integers: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100. (ii) Find the sum of the first 22 terms of the AP: 8, 3, -2, ...
worked_examples.given: (i) Natural numbers 1 to 100 (a = 1, l = 100, n = 100). (ii) AP: a = 8, d = -5, n = 22.
worked_examples.calculation:
Part (i):
Step 1: Write S forward and backward:
  S = 1 + 2 + ... + 99 + 100
  S = 100 + 99 + ... + 2 + 1
Step 2: Add vertically: 2*S = (1+100) + (2+99) + ... + (100+1) = 100 * 101 = 10,100.
Step 3: Divide by 2: S = 10,100 / 2 = 5,050.

Part (ii):
Step 1: First term a = 8, common difference d = 3 - 8 = -5, number of terms n = 22.
Step 2: Substitute into formula:
  S_22 = (22 / 2) * [2 * 8 + (22 - 1) * (-5)]
  S_22 = 11 * [16 + 21 * (-5)]
  S_22 = 11 * [16 - 105]
  S_22 = 11 * [-89]
  S_22 = -979.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (i) Sum of first 100 integers = 5,050; (ii) Sum of first 22 terms = -979

title: Geometric Progressions (GP): Common Ratio, Exponential Growth & The Sierpiński Fractal
description: Explore geometric progressions where each term is multiplied by a constant ratio r. Formulate the general term t_n = a * r^{n-1}. Model bouncing ball damping curves and the self-similar Sierpiński triangle fractal.
subtopics: Formal definition of a GP: t_{n+1} / t_n = r (constant common ratio)
Exponential vs linear growth: Comparing AP common difference with GP ratio
General term formula: t_n = a * r^{n-1}
Fractional and negative common ratios: Oscillating and decaying sequences
Bouncing ball damping model: Successive heights h_n = h_0 * r^n
Fun with Fractals (Section 8.6.1): The Sierpiński Triangle Area GP
key_concepts: Common Ratio Invariant: In a GP, the quotient of any term by its predecessor is constant: r = t_{k+1} / t_k.
GP General Term Formula: t_n = a * r^{n-1}. Growth is exponential because the variable n appears in the exponent.
Bouncing Ball Exponential Decay: A ball dropped from height h_0 that rebounds to a fraction r of its previous height reaches height h_n = h_0 * r^n on the nth bounce.

Sierpiński Triangle Fractal Invariants: At stage n, the number of solid triangles is 3^n (a GP with ratio 3), the area of each triangle is (1/4)^n A_0 (a GP with ratio 1/4), and the total shaded area is (3/4)^n A_0 (a decaying GP with ratio 3/4 approaching 0 as n -> infty).
success_criteria: Verify if sequences are GPs, compute general terms with fractional/negative ratios, and calculate fractal properties.
chapter_notes: Fractals in Section 8.6.1 demonstrate the beauty of math. Show how removing the central upside-down triangle creates 3 smaller copies, leading directly to the (3/4)^n area progression.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Exercise 8.3 Q1 & Q2: (Q1) Find the 12th term of a GP with common ratio 2 whose 8th term is 192. (Q2) Find the 10th and nth terms of the GP: 5, 25, 125, ...
worked_examples.calculation:
Part (Q1):
Step 1: Relate t_12 directly to t_8 using the common ratio:
  t_8 = a * r^7 = 192
  t_12 = a * r^11 = (a * r^7) * r^4 = t_8 * r^4.
Step 2: Substitute values:
  t_12 = 192 * 2^4 = 192 * 16.
Step 3: Perform multiplication:
  192 * 16 = 192 * (10 + 6) = 1920 + 1152 = 3,072.

Part (Q2):
Step 1: First term a = 5, common ratio r = 25 / 5 = 5.
Step 2: General term:
  t_n = a * r^{n-1} = 5 * 5^{n-1} = 5^{1 + n - 1} = 5^n.
Step 3: 10th term:
  t_10 = 5^10 = (5^2)^5 = 25^5 = 9,765,625.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Section 8.6.1 Fractal Problem: In the Sierpiński triangle, stage 0 is an equilateral triangle of area 64 cm^2. At each stage, the central inverted triangle is removed. Find: (i) the total remaining shaded area at Stage 1, Stage 2, and Stage 3, (ii) the formula for the shaded area at Stage n.
worked_examples.given: Stage 0 Area A_0 = 64 cm^2. At each stage, 1/4 of each triangle is removed, leaving 3/4 of the area.
worked_examples.formula: Shaded Area at Stage n: A_n = A_0 * (3/4)^n.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Stage 1 (n = 1):
  A_1 = 64 * (3/4) = 16 * 3 = 48 cm^2.
Step 2: Stage 2 (n = 2):
  A_2 = 64 * (9/16) = 4 * 9 = 36 cm^2.
Step 3: Stage 3 (n = 3):
  A_3 = 64 * (27/64) = 27 cm^2.
Step 4: Stage n general formula:
  A_n = 64 * (3/4)^n cm^2.
  As n approaches infinity, (3/4)^n approaches 0, meaning the Sierpiński triangle has ZERO area but INFINITE perimeter!
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Stage 1 = 48 cm^2; Stage 2 = 36 cm^2; Stage 3 = 27 cm^2; Formula A_n = 64 * (3/4)^n cm^2

common_misconceptions: Writing the GP general term as a * r^n instead of a * r^{n-1}.
Assuming fractal area increases because the number of triangles grows from 1 to 3 to 9 to 27 (the total area DECREASES because each triangle shrinks faster than the count grows).

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 8.1 Q2: Find the 10th and 15th terms of the sequence whose nth term is given by t_n = 5n - 3 for n >= 1. Also write the recursive rule for this sequence.
worked_examples.formula: t_n = 5n - 3. First term a = t_1. Recursive rule: t_{n+1} = t_n + d.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Compute 10th term:
  t_10 = 5 * 10 - 3 = 50 - 3 = 47.
Step 2: Compute 15th term:
  t_15 = 5 * 15 - 3 = 75 - 3 = 72.
Step 3: Determine the first term and common difference:
  t_1 = 5(1) - 3 = 2
  t_2 = 5(2) - 3 = 7
  Common difference d = 7 - 2 = 5.
Step 4: Formulate recursive rule:
  Base case: t_1 = 2
  Inductive step: t_{n+1} = t_n + 5 for n >= 1.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: t_10 = 47, t_15 = 72; Recursive rule: t_1 = 2, t_{n+1} = t_n + 5

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 8.2 Q3: Find the nth term of the AP: 11, 8, 5, 2, ... and write down its recursive rule.
worked_examples.formula: First term a = 11, d = t_2 - t_1. General term t_n = a + (n - 1)d.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Find common difference:
  d = 8 - 11 = -3.
  Verify: 5 - 8 = -3; 2 - 5 = -3. (Constant difference -3 confirmed!)
Step 2: Apply general term formula:
  t_n = a + (n - 1)d
  t_n = 11 + (n - 1)(-3)
  t_n = 11 - 3n + 3
  t_n = 14 - 3n.
Step 3: Write recursive rule:
  Initial condition: t_1 = 11
  Recursive step: t_{n+1} = t_n - 3 for n >= 1.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: General term: t_n = 14 - 3n; Recursive rule: t_1 = 11, t_{n+1} = t_n - 3

common_misconceptions: Expanding 11 + (n - 1)(-3) as 11 - 3n - 3 instead of + 3 (negative times negative is positive: -1 * -3 = +3).
Leaving out the base condition t_1 = 11 when specifying a recursive rule.

Term Exceeding Invariant: The statement 'the 7th term exceeds the 5th term by 12' translates directly to: t_7 - t_5 = 12 => [a + 6d] - [a + 4d] = 12 => 2d = 12 => d = 6.
Nonlinear Recurrence Trajectory: The rule t_{n+1} = 3t_n - 2 with t_1 = 2 yields: t_2 = 3(2) - 2 = 4, t_3 = 3(4) - 2 = 10, t_4 = 3(10) - 2 = 28. Notice differences are powers of 3: 2, 6, 18...

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Q1: Find the 31st term of an AP whose 11th term is 38 and 16th term is 73.
worked_examples.formula: t_n = a + (n - 1)d. Set up two simultaneous linear equations.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Write the two equations:
  a + 10d = 38 ... (Equation 1)
  a + 15d = 73 ... (Equation 2)
Step 2: Subtract Equation 1 from Equation 2:
  (a + 15d) - (a + 10d) = 73 - 38
  5d = 35
  d = 35 / 5 = 7.
Step 3: Substitute d = 7 into Equation 1 to find a:
  a + 10(7) = 38
  a + 70 = 38
  a = 38 - 70 = -32.
Step 4: Compute the 31st term t_31:
  t_31 = a + (31 - 1)d
  t_31 = -32 + 30 * (7)
  t_31 = -32 + 210 = 178.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: First term a = -32, Common difference d = 7; 31st term = 178

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Q2: Determine the AP whose third term is 16 and whose 7th term exceeds the 5th term by 12.
worked_examples.calculation:
Step 1: Analyze the difference condition:
  t_7 - t_5 = 12
  [a + 6d] - [a + 4d] = 12
  2d = 12
  d = 12 / 2 = 6.
Step 2: Use the third term equation to find a:
  a + 2d = 16
  a + 2(6) = 16
  a + 12 = 16
  a = 16 - 12 = 4.
Step 3: Construct the AP sequence:
  t_1 = a = 4
  t_2 = a + d = 4 + 6 = 10
  t_3 = a + 2d = 4 + 12 = 16
  t_4 = a + 3d = 4 + 18 = 22
  AP: 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, ...
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The AP is: 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, ... (with a = 4 and d = 6)

questions.question: Determine whether the sequence given by t_1 = 2, t_{n+1} = 3t_n - 2 is an AP, a GP, or neither.
questions.ideal_answer: Compute terms: t_1 = 2. t_2 = 3(2) - 2 = 4. t_3 = 3(4) - 2 = 10. t_4 = 3(10) - 2 = 28. Check AP: 4 - 2 = 2, but 10 - 4 = 6 (not constant, not an AP). Check GP: 4/2 = 2, but 10/4 = 2.5 (not constant, not a GP). Therefore, it is NEITHER an AP nor a GP (it is an arithmetic-geometric recurrence).
questions.socratic_hint: Check if consecutive differences are constant (AP) or consecutive ratios are constant (GP).
